scenes.title: Propositions and Truth Tables
scenes.summary:
Switch the connective and a new truth-table column fills in. All four cases sit side by side for comparison.

Two statements with identical columns mean the same thing. If the true rows and false rows match completely, the statements are equivalent. A statement and its contrapositive always match. The converse does not.

For example, 'if it rains, the ground gets wet' and 'if the ground is not wet, it did not rain' say the same thing. But 'if the ground is wet, it rained' can be false. A hose wets the ground too.

scenes.title: Universal and Existential Quantifiers
scenes.summary:
A game on the number line teaches the quantifiers. Swap the order and watch the same game collapse.

One side moves first and the other side answers. 'For all' demands an answer to every challenge. 'There exists' needs just one good answer. Swapping the order changes the claim itself. This pattern becomes the epsilon-delta definition later.

For example, for every 🧑 classmate, someone taller exists. But one person taller than everybody does not exist. A single swap changes the whole meaning.

scenes.title: Direct Proof
scenes.summary:
Place the sum of two rationals on the number line and follow the computation. It runs straight from hypothesis to conclusion.

A direct proof walks straight ahead. Compute with what you are given and the conclusion falls out. Fractions combine over a common denominator into one fraction. So a sum of rationals is rational again.

For example, take three quarters of a 🍰 cake and remove five sixths of one. Recut into twelfths: nine pieces minus ten pieces. One straight computation, no detours.

scenes.title: Proof by Contrapositive
scenes.summary:
Lay out an even-odd table and set a statement beside its contrapositive. This is the detour for when the direct road is blocked.

Some statements resist a frontal attack. Then flip and negate: prove the contrapositive instead. It always shares the original's truth value. Settle one side and the other comes free.

For example, if a square is even, the number itself is even. Instead of studying squares, look only at odd numbers. Squaring an odd number always gives an odd number. So an even square never came from an odd number.

scenes.title: Proof by Contradiction
scenes.summary:
Assume there are only finitely many primes and derive a contradiction. Watch a new prime slip outside the list.

Proof by contradiction assumes the opposite side. Push the false side until it clashes with itself. Then the original claim must be true. Multiplying all the primes and adding one builds that clash.

For example, suppose a biggest number exists. Add one and a bigger number appears. The assumption destroys itself. Euclid's prime proof uses exactly this move.

scenes.title: Proof by Cases and Existence Proofs
scenes.summary:
Split the plane into four regions and handle one case at a time. Then meet a proof that shows existence without revealing which side holds.

A case split must leave no gap. Each region's computation is easy. Miss one region and the whole proof collapses. Existence proofs are different: 'it exists' can be shown without producing it.

For example, a 🧑 friend may stand east or west of your house. Either way, the distance home ignores the sign. Checking both directions is exactly a proof by cases.

scenes.title: Counterexamples and If and Only If
scenes.summary:
Demolish false claims with a single counterexample. Four plausible claims go on trial, one by one.

A 'for all' claim falls to one counterexample. A single failing case makes the whole claim false. An if-and-only-if claim is the opposite job. Each direction needs its own separate proof.

For example, take 'every 🧑 classmate wears glasses'. One classmate without glasses ends the claim. One person is enough.

scenes.title: Strong Induction
scenes.summary:
Draw the tree that splits a number into prime factors. It shows why the proof must assume everything before it.

Ordinary induction uses only the step right before. But split-off pieces land far below, not one step down. Strong induction assumes every earlier step at once. Each piece counts as already settled on the way up.

For example, climbing 🪜 stairs, some steps push off two or three steps below. Trusting only the step right beneath you is not always enough. Trust them all, and the next step holds.

scenes.title: Equivalence Relations
scenes.summary:
Group numbers by equal remainders. Then test three promises on everything to certify an equivalence relation.

An equivalence relation means 'on the same team'. Everyone is on their own team. Teaming is mutual, and it chains through teammates. When all three hold, the whole set splits into non-overlapping teams.

For example, split twelve 🧑 classmates into three teams of four. Nobody belongs to two teams at once. Inside a team, everyone matches everyone. Remainder classes look exactly like this.

scenes.title: Proofs about Composite Functions
scenes.summary:
Glue two functions together and inspect the composite with tables and arrows. See what the composite's properties force onto each part.

If the composite is injective, the first function is injective too. If the composite is surjective, the second function is surjective. The converses fail, and the diagrams show why. Undoing a composite also reverses the order.

For example, pack a 📦 box, close the lid, then tie it with string. To open it, the string comes off first. The last step done is the first step undone. That is why inverses of composites reverse the order.

scenes.title: Natural Numbers and Induction
scenes.summary:
Watch the natural numbers being born from axioms. Line up dominoes to see induction start.

Induction proves infinitely many statements at once. Check the first case. Then show each case hands truth to the next. The chain never ends, so everything holds.

For example, stand on the first 🪜 stair and know how to climb one more. The first step plus the climbing rule reaches the top. Dominoes fall the same way.

scenes.title: The Binomial Theorem
scenes.summary:
See the triangle made by the coefficients of expanded powers. Follow one whole row being computed.

A binomial coefficient counts ways to choose. Each entry in the triangle is the sum of the two above it. That addition rule is the heart of the induction step. A whole row adds up to a power of two.

For example, toss two coins and count the heads: zero, one, or two. The counts go one way, two ways, one way. That is the triangle's second row, exactly.

scenes.title: Integers and Rationals
scenes.summary:
Build negative numbers and fractions by bundling pairs. Pairs naming the same number form one bundle.

Integers are bundles of pairs of naturals. Fractions are bundles of pairs of integers. Different pairs can name the same number. This bundle trick returns when the reals are built.

For example, think of 💰 money and debt. Five coins in hand and three owed is a net of two. Seven in hand and five owed is also two. Different pairs, same value.

scenes.title: Complex Numbers
scenes.summary:
See a complex number as a point in the plane. The real part runs sideways, the imaginary part runs up.

The modulus is the distance from the origin to that point. Adding two complex numbers draws the diagonal of a parallelogram. That diagonal is never longer than the two sides added together. This is the triangle inequality.

For example, walk 3 steps east with a 🧭 compass, then turn and walk 4 more. The straight-line distance back is shorter than the bent path. The modulus measures exactly that straight line.

scenes.title: √2 is Irrational
scenes.summary:
Plot fractions ever more densely and watch one hole never fill. That spot is the square root of two.

Rationals alone do not complete the number line. No fraction squares to exactly two. However fine the denominators, that spot stays empty. Numbers beyond the rationals are needed.

For example, measure a length with a 📏 ruler. However fine the marks, some lengths never match one. A square's diagonal is such a length. Fraction marks never catch it.

scenes.title: Density of the Rationals
scenes.summary:
See that every interval, however narrow, hides a rational. Bigger denominators make the ticks denser.

Between any two numbers sits a fraction. Narrower gaps need bigger denominators. Chop the scale finely enough and some tick lands in every gap. The same trick works around irrationals.

For example, keep cutting a 🍰 cake in half, again and again. The pieces shrink without end. Pick any thin gap, and a thinner piece exists. That piece is the fraction landing inside.

scenes.title: Sets and Functions
scenes.summary:
Overlap sets in pictures to see unions and intersections. Judge by eye whether a map is injective or surjective.

A union takes anything in at least one set. An intersection needs both. A complement is everything outside. Colliding or missing arrows decide injective versus surjective.

For example, some 🧑 classmates love 📚 books, while others love ⚽ soccer. Friends loving both stand in the overlap. Loving at least one puts you in the union.

scenes.title: The Axiom of Choice
scenes.summary:
Pick one dot from each row of a table. See why finite collections and infinite ones differ.

The question is whether picking can be made into a function. Finitely many sets: just pick, one by one. Infinitely many: the picking rule itself needs a guarantee. That guarantee is the axiom of choice.

For example, every 📦 box holds some 🍬 candies. With three boxes, just reach in and pick. With endless boxes, you need the rule 'one from each box'. Nobody can check them all by eye.

scenes.title: Zorn's Lemma
scenes.summary:
Stand the divisors of twelve in divisibility order. Climb a chain and see what sits at the top.

A chain is a line of mutually comparable elements. If every chain has an upper bound, a maximal element exists. You never construct it; existence is guaranteed. The guarantee matches the axiom of choice.

For example, the top of a 🪜 staircase has no next step. Every way up ends somewhere. Knowing every climb ends proves a top exists.

scenes.title: The Supremum Axiom
scenes.summary:
Find the smallest ceiling over a bounded set. That ceiling, missing in the rationals, completes the reals.

The supremum is the least of all upper bounds. Ceilings are many, but the lowest one is unique. Rationals sometimes lack that lowest ceiling. The reals are the world where it always exists.

For example, measure every 🧑 classmate's height. The smallest line above them all is the supremum. It touches the tallest height exactly. Everyone fits underneath.

scenes.title: Existence of n-th Roots
scenes.summary:
Locate the point whose power hits the target, using a supremum. Watch the gap-filling axiom manufacture a root.

Collect every number whose power stays below the target. The supremum of that set is the root. Below it, powers fall short; above it, they overshoot. So the supremum's power equals the target exactly.

For example, find the side of a square with area two. Side one gives too little area; side two gives too much. One borderline length fits exactly. That length is the square root of two.

scenes.title: Countable vs Uncountable
scenes.summary:
See the rationals numbered in a single list. Then see the same attempt fail for the reals.

Countable means pairing off with the natural numbers. Fractions tile a grid, and a zigzag count numbers them all. Reals refuse. Every proposed list misses some real. Changing digits along the diagonal proves it.

For example, hand number tickets to every 🧑 classmate. However long the line, one ticket each means countable. If every roster still misses someone, the crowd cannot be counted.

scenes.title: Cantor's Theorem
scenes.summary:
See that any set is smaller than the collection of all its subsets. Flip a list's diagonal to build a new element.

The power set collects all subsets. One extra element doubles the subsets. So any attempted pairing leaves leftovers. The diagonal-flipped set is exactly such a leftover.

For example, three 🧑 classmates have eight subsets. Subsets already outnumber the friends. More people only widens the gap. Even infinity keeps the gap.

scenes.title: Groups vs Fields
scenes.summary:
Check the rules of reversible moves in a table. Compare with a world where all four operations work.

A group rests on three promises. Grouping must not change results. A do-nothing element must exist. Every move needs an undoing move. A field adds division on top of that.

For example, pedaling a bicycle forward can be undone by pedaling back. Staying still counts as a move too. Chaining moves gives another move. A set of moves obeying these rules is a group.

scenes.title: Vector Spaces and Isomorphism
scenes.summary:
Move the coefficients and watch a line and a point move together. Spaces with different looks share one structure.

A vector space supports adding and scaling. Pairs of numbers, polynomials, and functions all obey the same rules. Same rules means essentially the same world. Calculations transfer from one side to the other.

For example, write a recipe on a card. The card's numbers rebuild the dish exactly. A line, too, is captured by two numbers: slope and intercept. Card and line move as one.

scenes.title: Dimension and Rank
scenes.summary:
Watch a grid get squeezed flat by a matrix. Count the dimensions that vanish and those that survive.

Dimension counts independent directions. A matrix can squash directions together. Directions crushed to nothing form the kernel's dimension. Directions still spanning room form the rank. The two add up to the original dimension.

For example, sunlight presses a solid object into a flat shadow. The height direction vanishes in the shadow. Only the flat directions survive. Lost plus surviving equals the original dimension.

scenes.title: The ε–N Definition
scenes.summary:
Narrow the ε-band as much as you like: from some moment on, the whole tail sits inside it. This scene watches that moment arrive.

Converging means closing in on the target value without end. A narrower band only delays the moment the tail fits inside. As long as that moment always comes, the sequence converges. The exact promise is the formula below.

For example, a ⚽ ball rolled toward a line stops closer and closer to it. Demand it land within 10 cm, then within 1 cm — from some roll on, it always stays inside.

scenes.title: Standard Limits: x^n and x^{1/n}
scenes.summary:
Powers of a number below 1 in absolute value, and roots of a positive number, take the stage. The scene checks where each of them gathers.

Keep multiplying a number below 1 and it sinks toward 0. Take roots of a positive number again and again and it gathers at 1. At −1 the sign just flips back and forth. Beyond 1 in size, powers grow without end. Bernoulli's inequality handles every case.

For example, eat half of the remaining 🍰 cake each day. What is left goes one half, one quarter, one eighth — nearly vanishing.

scenes.title: Norm: The Rule for Measuring Length
scenes.summary:
How do we measure the length of a vector? The measuring rule is the norm.

The rule has three parts. A length is never negative, and only the zero vector has length 0. Scaling a vector scales its length by the same factor. And the length of a sum never exceeds the sum of the lengths. That last rule is the triangle inequality. Change the ruler and the length changes: the block-counting ruler, the straight-line ruler, and the king-move ruler all differ.

For example, in a 🏙 grid city, go one block east and one block north. The straight line is one diagonal, but on blocks you must walk twice. A chess king goes diagonally in one move. The same move measures 2, about 1.41, and 1 under the three rulers.

scenes.title: Sequence and Function Spaces
scenes.summary:
Whole sequences get collected into a single space here. Each sequence becomes one point of the space.

Sequences can be added and scaled, so the space is a vector space. The distance between two sequences can also be measured. The measuring rule decides which space a sequence fits into. A finite sum of absolute values fits the smallest space. A finite sum of squares fits the middle one. Merely being bounded fits the largest one. So each smaller space sits inside the bigger ones. The norm behind the distance bridges the two worlds. That these spaces are complete is stated as a known theorem only.

For example, picture three nested 📦 boxes. Anything inside the small box also lies in the middle and the large one. Sequence spaces nest in exactly the same way.

scenes.title: Cauchy–Schwarz Inequality
scenes.summary:
How large can the inner product of two vectors become? It can never exceed the product of the two norms.

The inner product measures how much one vector overlaps the other's direction. The overlap is largest when the two vectors point the same way. Tilt them apart and the overlap falls below the product of the norms. The proof starts from one fact: a length is never negative. Reading that fact as a discriminant drops the inequality out. Equality holds only when the two vectors are parallel.

For example, shine a light on a ✏️ pencil and its shadow is never longer than the pencil. Only when the pencil lines up with the light does the shadow match its full length.

scenes.title: Hölder’s Inequality
scenes.summary:
This scene widens Cauchy–Schwarz to general exponents. The key is that the two exponents come as a matched pair.

Multiply two sequences term by term and add them up: even that total has a ceiling. The ceiling is the product of the two sequences' norms. With both exponents equal to 2, it is exactly Cauchy–Schwarz. The key step is Young's inequality, which trades a product for shares of a sum. The precise formulas are below.

For example, at a 🏪 shop you multiply each item's price by its quantity and add everything up. That total never exceeds the product of the price list's size and the quantity list's size.

scenes.title: The Parallelogram Law
scenes.summary:
An identity hides between the two diagonals and the two sides of a parallelogram. This scene slides the exponent p and checks when that identity survives.

Every norm that comes from an inner product satisfies the identity. Computing with e_1 and e_2 makes the left side 2 \cdot 2^{2/p} and the right side 4. The two agree only at p = 2. So an \ell^p norm with p different from 2 cannot come from any inner product.

For example, a 📐 parallelogram drawn with a ruler stays exactly the same, but the measuring ruler is swapped. If swapping the ruler alone breaks the diagonal identity, that ruler never came from an inner-product blueprint.

scenes.title: Why ℝ Has No Holes
scenes.summary:
A sequence built only from rationals creeps toward a place that is not rational. The scene shows the hole in the rational world.

The iteration halves the error of each guess. Every term stays rational. Yet the destination is not a rational number. So rationals alone cannot fill that spot. The full irrationality proof is skipped; only the idea is shown.

For example, measure the diagonal of a square with a 📏 ruler. Try 1.4, then 1.41, then 1.414 — no fraction ever fits it exactly. That spot is the hole in the rationals.

scenes.title: Construction of the Real Numbers
scenes.summary:
The hole in the rationals gets filled and a real number is actually built. One real number is defined as a bundle of rational sequences.

Lengthen the decimal expansion and the rational terms march into the hole. Sequences whose difference vanishes count as the same number. That bundle itself is one real number. Built this way, the number line ends up with no holes. Completeness is exactly what this construction buys.

For example, climb a 🪜 staircase one step at a time toward the top. The numbers 1, 1.4, 1.41, 1.414 are footprints heading upward. The whole parade of footprints is the destination itself: the real number.

scenes.title: A Convergent Subsequence Always Hides Inside
scenes.summary:
Every bounded sequence hides a convergent subsequence inside it. This scene finds that subsequence by halving the interval.

The trick is to keep halving the interval. Always follow the half that holds infinitely many terms. Each halving makes the interval narrower. The points trapped inside pile onto a single value. Stringing those points together gives a convergent subsequence.

For example, thirty 🧑 classmates scatter across a playground. Split the playground in half and one side still holds a crowd of them. Keep halving that side and you corner a single spot.

scenes.title: Monotone and Cauchy Sequences
scenes.summary:
An increasing sequence blocked from above climbs to the very top. The scene also watches the tail squeeze into a single point.

Bounded above, the sequence has nowhere to go but its highest allowed spot. That spot is the supremum, and the sequence converges to it. Cut to the tail and the remaining terms spread less and less. A sequence whose spread dies to 0 is a Cauchy sequence. Every convergent sequence is Cauchy.

For example, drop coins into a 🐷 piggy bank: half the goal, then half of what remains, and so on. The total creeps toward the goal without ever jumping to it. The coins added later also differ from each other less and less.

scenes.title: Lim sup and Lim inf
scenes.summary:
Watch only the tails of a sequence and track their highest and lowest values. The scene checks where the two of them settle.

The supremum of the tails keeps stepping down, and the infimum keeps stepping up. The upper settling point is the lim sup, the lower one the lim inf. If the two meet, the limit exists. An oscillating sequence keeps them apart forever. The precise definitions are the formulas below.

For example, record each day's high and low temperature with a 🌡️ thermometer. As days pass, the highs gather near one value and the lows near another. If the two values coincide, the weather has settled on a single temperature.

scenes.title: Stolz–Cesàro Theorem
scenes.summary:
When the full ratio is stubborn, this scene detours through the ratio of differences. It is the sequence version of l'Hôpital's rule.

Compare the growth of single steps, and that ratio settles first. The full ratio follows slowly from behind. The denominator must increase strictly and grow without bound. Both ratios share the same destination. The headline example's limit is the second formula below.

For example, on a 🚗 car trip the speed over the last minute settles at 60 km/h. Then the average speed over the whole trip gets dragged toward 60 km/h as well.

scenes.title: Double Sequences and Iterated Limits
scenes.summary:
This scene is about double sequences. Watch the values a_{m,n} on a grid, and see how the row-wise and column-wise limits split apart.

The double limit lets both indices grow together. An iterated limit sends one index first, then the other. Swapping the order can change the answer. And even when both iterated limits agree, the double limit may not exist.

For example, reading a 📋 table row by row is not the same as reading it column by column. Change the reading order, and you can land on a completely different conclusion.

scenes.title: The ε–δ Definition
scenes.summary:
This scene makes the limit definition visible. It stacks an ε-band over a δ-band and grid-checks that the promise really holds.

The order is the point. First, someone else picks the allowed error. Then you must find a matching input window. If the input stays in that window, the output stays in the error band. The formula below states the promise. For the line here, a window of half the error is enough.

For example, play at throwing a ⚽ ball into a 📦 box. Your friend may swap in a smaller and smaller box. Standing close enough, you can still make every throw. The smaller the box, the closer you must stand.

scenes.title: The Definition of Continuity
scenes.summary:
This scene shows what continuity means at a point. Move the point a, then lift one value and watch continuity break.

There is one condition. The height you approach must equal the height at the point. Changing a single value breaks that agreement. The graph then tears at that point.

For example, draw the graph with a ✏️ pencil without lifting it. If one stroke suffices, the function is continuous. If one point floats above the rest, you must lift the pencil there.

scenes.title: Thomae's Function
scenes.summary:
This scene shows Thomae's function, a popcorn of dots. Dots jump up at rationals and stick to the floor at irrationals.

Tall dots are rare. Fix any height: only finitely many dots reach it. So near an irrational you can choose a window avoiding tall dots. That is why it is continuous at irrationals only.

For example, picture a jar of 🍬 candies. Only a few are big, and you can count them. A corner with only tiny candies is nearly flat. Neighborhoods of irrationals look like that: no big jumps, so the function stays quiet.

scenes.title: Three Faces of Continuity
scenes.summary:
This scene checks continuity in three different ways. The ε–δ argument, the sequential test, and preimages of open sets stand side by side.

The three faces say the same thing. Bands, sequences, or pulled-back open sets all give the same verdict. A smooth curve passes all three. A jump function fails all three at the same spot.

For example, look at one object in a 🪞 mirror from three sides. Front or side, it is the same object. Continuity is like that: many checks, one question.

scenes.title: Discontinuities of Monotone Functions
scenes.summary:
This scene inspects the discontinuities of a monotone function. It only ever climbs, so every break is a jump.

Big jumps are few. The total climb is fixed, and that bounds them. Set a threshold: only finitely many jumps exceed it. Lowering the threshold step by step counts all discontinuities.

For example, take a 🪜 staircase three meters tall in total. Steps higher than 30 cm number at most nine. Counting steps down to 3 cm changes nothing: many steps, still countable one by one.

scenes.title: Uniform Continuity
scenes.summary:
This scene tests uniform continuity. Slide the point x and watch how the δ it needs changes from point to point.

Ordinary continuity lets δ depend on the point. Uniform continuity demands one δ working everywhere. Where the curve steepens, the needed δ keeps shrinking. If it steepens forever, no single δ can cover everything.

For example, imagine a whole class sharing one 📏 ruler. Everyone must measure with that same ruler. If it is too short for even one person's turn, the measurement fails there.

scenes.title: You Can't Climb Without Crossing Every Height
scenes.summary:
This scene checks the intermediate value theorem. Move the target height and find where the graph crosses it.

An unbroken path cannot skip the middle. Going from low to high, it must pass every height between. If the graph breaks, the promise fails.

For example, watch the column of a 🌡️ thermometer. Rising from 10° in the morning to 20° at noon, it must pass 15°. The column never teleports.

scenes.title: The Extreme Value Theorem
scenes.summary:
This scene checks the extreme value theorem. On a closed interval the maximum is attained; open intervals and breaks show why it can fail.

Two conditions are needed. The interval must be closed, and the graph must be unbroken. Drop either one, and the highest point may only be approached, never reached. That is why both hypotheses matter.

For example, picture a 🧑 hiker walking a trail to the summit. If the trail runs all the way, some step lands on the highest point. If the trail breaks just before it, the hiker gets close but never arrives.

scenes.title: When the Limit Breaks
scenes.summary:
This scene separates pointwise from uniform convergence. Watch the power curves break in the limit.

Pointwise convergence waits at each point separately. Uniform convergence moves the whole interval at once. If even one point holds out forever, convergence is not uniform. That is how a limit of continuous curves can break.

For example, picture 🧑 classmates in a row sitting down together. It counts as done only when everyone is seated. If one classmate stays standing, the row as a whole is not finished.

scenes.title: Open and Closed Sets
scenes.summary:
This scene shows what an open set is. Move the point and the radius, and check whether the small ball fits inside.

Open means no point clings to the boundary. Around every point there is a small interval lying inside the set. At a boundary point, every interval, however small, pokes outside.

For example, kick a ⚽ ball in the middle of a yard. A gentle kick keeps it inside. Kick from right at the fence, and it flies out at once. That is the difference between an interior point and a boundary point.

scenes.title: Clopen Sets
scenes.summary:
This scene is about sets both open and closed: clopen sets. The same set changes its fate with the space it lives in.

On the whole real line, only the empty set and the line itself qualify. A boundary always appears somewhere. But if the space splits into two separate pieces, one piece touches no boundary. That piece is both open and closed.

For example, take one of two far-apart 🏠 houses. In a world made of that house alone, it forms its own separate region. It is open, and it is closed.

scenes.title: Connected Sets
scenes.summary:
This scene is about connected sets. Move the cut point and check whether the set splits into two open pieces that never touch.

A set that cannot be split is connected. An interval never splits: wherever you cut, the cut point itself belongs to neither side. Two far-apart pieces, or the rationals with their dense gaps, split cleanly when the cut lands in a gap.

For example, look at one 🧩 jigsaw puzzle. While the pieces interlock, it is a single board. Lying in two completely separate piles, it is already split apart.

scenes.title: Closure and Boundedness
scenes.summary:
This scene builds the closure of a set. Watch what happens when every escaped limit point is pulled back in.

The closure contains every point the set was reaching for. If some point is approached but never touched, closing means adding it. A set already holding all its limit points equals its closure. Add boundedness, and compactness is near.

For example, fill a 📦 box and put the lid on. Only with the lid is the box complete. Closure is like that lid: it adds the boundary points to the set.

scenes.title: Compact Sets
scenes.summary:
This scene tests compactness with open covers. See whether finitely many covering pieces always suffice.

Compact means closed and bounded together. An open end needs endless pieces near the gap. An endless stretch fails the same way. With both conditions, any cover shrinks to finitely many pieces.

For example, cover a desk completely with 📚 books. A finite desk needs only a few books. An endless desk would defeat any pile, however large.

scenes.title: Topologist's Sine Curve
scenes.summary:
This scene draws the topologist's sine curve. Watch it oscillate endlessly near zero, and the limit segment it sticks to.

The closer to zero, the faster the curve wiggles. So a whole segment on the axis sticks to the curve. The combined figure is in one piece. Yet no path walks from the segment into the curve. Being in one piece and having a path are different things.

For example, shake one end of a 🧵 string faster and faster. The shaking end blurs into a band. The band is visible, but you cannot walk from one point of it onto a chosen part of the string.

scenes.title: Peano Curve
scenes.summary:
This scene builds the Peano curve, one line filling a square. Watch the approximations grow denser at every stage.

The curve folds like a snake, filling the gaps. More folds mean more points touched. In the limit it passes through every point of the square. But it must visit some points twice. So no injective filling exists.

For example, color a whole sheet with a ✏️ pencil, never lifting it. Zigzag densely back and forth, and eventually every point is touched. One line fills an entire surface.

scenes.title: Metric Spaces
scenes.summary:
This scene axiomatizes distance. Compare how the shape of a ball changes when the metric changes.

A metric obeys only three rules. Distances are never negative. The distance is the same both ways. A detour is never shorter than the direct way. Same rules, different measurement: balls of equal radius take different shapes.

For example, change how a 📏 ruler measures between two points. Measure straight, and you get a disk. Measure along grid lines only, and you get a diamond. Same radius, different reach.

scenes.title: Contraction Mapping Principle
scenes.summary:
This scene runs the contraction mapping principle. Iterate and watch the points tighten onto one fixed point.

A contraction shrinks every distance by one fixed ratio. Iterating pulls all points toward each other. Every start leads to the same destination. But if the space has a hole, the destination can fall into it.

For example, fold a 🗺️ map in half, then in half again. Each fold shrinks the paper, and all points gather toward one. That point is the fixed point. Tear a hole in the middle, and the gathering point is gone.

scenes.title: Baire Category Theorem
scenes.summary:
This scene follows the Baire category theorem through nested intervals. Dodge the rationals one by one, and a point still remains.

Sets full of holes cannot cover everything. Choose smaller and smaller closed intervals, each dodging the next bad point. The intervals tighten onto one point belonging to no hole set. A complete space always keeps such a point.

For example, put a 📦 box inside a box, then a smaller one inside that. However small it gets, room remains at the center. Choosing the boxes to dodge rationals still leaves one point standing.

scenes.title: Baire Class 1 Functions
scenes.summary:
This scene builds a Baire class 1 function. Thomae's function rises as a pointwise limit of continuous tent sums.

Stacking only continuous functions can still produce breaks. But the breaks cannot be everywhere. Points of continuity are always dense. Even a limit-made function keeps this much order.

For example, bend a 🧵 string into ever sharper mountain shapes. At every stage the string is unbroken. In the end, a row of thorn-like spikes remains.

scenes.title: Length Zero, Points Uncountable
scenes.summary:
This scene builds the Cantor set. Keep deleting middle thirds: the length dies to zero, yet uncountably many points survive.

Each deletion shrinks the total length to two-thirds. After infinitely many rounds, the length is zero. But some points are never cut away. There are as many of them as there are real numbers.

For example, cut the middle third out of a 🍰 cake. Then cut the middle of each remaining piece, again and again. The cake almost vanishes. Still, uncountably many spots were never touched by the knife.

scenes.title: The Fat Cantor Set
scenes.summary:
This scene builds the fat Cantor set. Dig out only a little at each stage, and half the length survives.

Digging less changes the outcome. The remaining set is still full of holes, with empty interior. Yet its length converges to one half. Size by length and size by topology are independent.

For example, scoop a 🍰 cake again, but take only small bites. Holes appear everywhere, yet half the cake remains to eat. It looks empty, but the amount is real.

scenes.title: The Cantor Function
scenes.summary:
This scene climbs the Cantor function, the Devil's staircase. It is continuous and always rising, yet flat on almost every interval.

The function pauses on every gap of the Cantor set. So its slope is zero at almost every point. And still it climbs from 0 to 1 overall. The total climb disagrees with the sum of slopes.

For example, climb a 🪜 staircase whose landings are endlessly long. You rest almost the whole way, yet you still reach the top. The Cantor function does exactly that.

scenes.title: Arzelà–Ascoli Theorem
scenes.summary:
When can we pull a uniformly convergent subsequence out of a family of continuous functions?

Two conditions do the job. First, every function stays inside one 📦 box. Second, all of them wiggle with similar gentleness. A diagonal argument over the rationals then builds a subsequence. It closes in everywhere at once. The power functions fail the second condition: they turn steep suddenly near 1.

For example, picture 30 🧑 friends walking across a playground. Everyone must stay inside the fence. Nobody may suddenly sprint. Then you can pick a group whose walks grow alike. One friend sprinting at the end ruins the group.

scenes.title: Weierstrass Approximation Theorem
scenes.summary:
Can polynomials alone imitate every continuous function on an interval?

A Bernstein polynomial averages the function's values near each point. As the degree grows, the average concentrates near that point. So the polynomial follows even the bumpy corners. The proof's fine estimates are only sketched.

For example, think of replacing a slope with a 🪜 staircase. The finer the steps, the smaller the gap anywhere you measure. Raising the degree presses the polynomial onto the whole function at once.

scenes.title: Stone–Weierstrass Theorem
scenes.summary:
Can materials other than polynomials approximate every continuous function?

The ingredient set needs three things. Closure under addition and multiplication. The power to tell two different points apart. And the constant functions. With only these, it tracks any continuous function as closely as you like.

For example, layering round waves can build even a pointy 🏠 roof shape. In this scene, waves of sines and cosines close in on the triangle wave on a circle.

scenes.title: Müntz–Szász Theorem
scenes.summary:
Can we skip some powers and still approximate everything?

The test is the sum of the reciprocals of the exponents. If that sum grows forever, the ingredients are dense enough. If it stays finite, some function remains forever out of reach. The scene fits the square-root function by least squares and compares a dense set with a sparse one.

For example, think of measuring with a 📏 ruler. Marks packed endlessly close let you measure any length well. Marks that thin out like 1, 4, 9 leave some lengths unmeasurable forever.

scenes.title: The Harmonic Series Diverges
scenes.summary:
The terms shrink to 0, yet the partial sums grow without end. The growth is just extremely slow.

Each single term is tiny, but the pile keeps rising. The partial sums climb upward along a logarithm curve. Terms tending to 0 do not guarantee that a series converges. This series is the classic counterexample.

For example, stack 🍬 candy pieces of one, a half, a third of a piece, and so on. The pieces keep shrinking, yet the pile eventually rises past any ceiling you name.

scenes.title: The Euler–Mascheroni Constant
scenes.summary:
Two quantities both diverge, yet the gap between them settles at one value. That gap is the Euler–Mascheroni constant.

The harmonic numbers and the logarithm both grow without end. Still, the space between them narrows and comes to a stop. The gap stops because its increments form a convergent series. That secret is the second formula below.

For example, two 🧑 friends run side by side. Both run endlessly far, but the distance between them stops growing at about 5 meters. That settled distance plays the role of this constant.

scenes.title: The Basel Problem
scenes.summary:
A staircase of reciprocal squares climbs toward one flat plane. The height of that plane is the famous answer.

Each new step of the partial sums is smaller than the one before. So the staircase piles up toward a definite height. The surprise is that π hides inside that height. Why π appears at all is only sketched at the idea level.

For example, stack 📦 boxes under a line drawn on a wall. The boxes shrink until the stack creeps so close to the line that your eye cannot see the gap.

scenes.title: The Euler Product
scenes.summary:
A series gets sieved until only the primes remain. The sum turns out to equal a product over all primes.

Multiply by the factor that erases the even terms, and the evens vanish. Multiply by the factor for multiples of 3, and those vanish too. Sieve once for each prime and only prime information survives. Even the product over the first few primes already lands close to the answer.

For example, line up 🍬 candies numbered from 1 onward. Remove the even numbers, then the multiples of 3, and only prime numbers stay. This sieving is what builds the product formula.

scenes.title: Leibniz Series
scenes.summary:
The partial sums overshoot the target, then undershoot it, closing in from both sides. It is a sandwich that keeps tightening.

Add one term and you jump past the target; the next term pulls you back. The back-and-forth swing shrinks every time. So the target always sits between two neighboring partial sums. That gap is exactly the error bound.

For example, a ⚽ ball rolls past a line, comes back, and crosses it again. Each crossing overshoots by less than the one before. The ball has no choice but to settle on the line.

scenes.title: Convergence Tests Toolbox
scenes.summary:
This scene opens the toolbox for deciding whether a series converges. Two representative tools get used directly.

The first tool watches the ratio of neighboring terms. If the ratio settles below 1, the terms shrink fast enough to converge. The second tool compares against a neighboring series. Anything tucked under a convergent series converges along with it. Both tools' formulas are below.

For example, hand out 🍬 candies each day, always half of yesterday's amount. When the amounts shrink by a fixed ratio, the total handed out stays finite. If the ratio refuses to shrink, the handing out never ends.

scenes.title: The Integral Test
scenes.summary:
A series and an integral get stacked together and share one fate. The bars wrap the curve from above and below.

Stand bars under a decreasing curve, and the sum traps the integral from both sides. So the series and the integral converge or diverge together. An exponent above 1 gives convergence; anything else diverges. That fork decides the fate of every p-series.

For example, stack 📚 books like steps against a ramp. The steps dip below the ramp's curve and poke above it. Still, the steps' area and the area under the curve are finite together or endless together.

scenes.title: Raabe's Test
scenes.summary:
Where the ratio test surrenders, this scene digs one level deeper. It is the tool for ratios that stick to 1.

Measure how fast the ratio approaches 1, and the verdict revives. The quantity doing the measuring is the first formula below. If it settles above 1, the series converges. If it settles below 1, the series diverges.

For example, a coarse 📏 ruler sometimes cannot separate two lengths. Switch to a ruler with finer marks, and the lengths finally split apart. Raabe's test is that finer ruler.

scenes.title: Kummer's Test
scenes.summary:
One big frame unifies several convergence tests in this scene. A single auxiliary sequence switches which test you get.

Weight the ratio to build a new quantity. The sign of that quantity decides convergence or divergence. Set every weight to 1 and you get the ratio test. Set the weights to the term index and you get Raabe's test. The precise formulas are below.

For example, turn a dial on a ⚙️ machine and the inspection strength changes. One position gives a weak check, another position a strong one. The auxiliary sequence is that dial.

scenes.title: Cauchy Condensation Test
scenes.summary:
Terms get grouped into blocks that double in size here. The grouped series and the original share their fate.

For a decreasing sequence, the terms inside one block all look alike. So each block sum is trapped between multiples of one representative term. Compressing each block into its representative leaves convergence unchanged. The test becomes far easier to run.

For example, pack 🍬 candies into boxes of 1, 2, 4, doubling each time. Judging each box by one representative candy does not change whether the total is finite.

scenes.title: Telescoping Series
scenes.summary:
Split each term and the neighbors erase each other in this scene. Only the very first piece and a vanishing tail survive.

Each term breaks into a difference of two fractions. The back half of one term matches the front half of the next, so they cancel. After the erasing, only the opening 1 remains. The tail shrinks away to nothing. So the total is exactly 1.

For example, climb one step of a 🪜 staircase and step back down: you are where you started. Chain these ups and downs together and only the starting and ending positions count.

scenes.title: Geometric Series: Filling the Square
scenes.summary:
A unit square gets filled by always taking half of what remains. The gap halves at every step and the total becomes 1.

Paint half, then paint half of the rest. The painted area creeps closer and closer to 1. However small the gap gets, one step always remains. In partial sums, that leftover step just keeps halving. Added forever, the pieces make exactly 1.

For example, eat half of a 🍰 cake, then half of what is left. The bites go one half, one quarter, one eighth, yet together they approach the whole cake.

scenes.title: Wallis Product
scenes.summary:
Rational factors get multiplied in one at a time here. The running product swings around one value, tightening as it goes.

The running product alternates above and below its target. The swings shrink as more factors pile in. So the product settles onto a single value. The surprise is that this value is π divided by 2.

For example, a 🚗 car eases into the center of its lane with small steering corrections to the left and right. Each correction is smaller than the last, and the car steadies in the middle.

scenes.title: Stirling's Approximation
scenes.summary:
A fast-growing factorial gets guessed by one simple formula here. On a log scale, the two curves nearly coincide.

Factorials grow too fast to keep computing head-on. The approximation tracks that growth almost exactly. Its relative error shrinks as the terms grow. Roughly, it falls like 1 over 12 times the index. Where π enters is only sketched at the idea level.

For example, guess a tall 🏢 building's height by counting steps. The taller the building, the smaller the share of one step's error in the whole. That is why the approximation sharpens for large numbers.

scenes.title: Grandi Series
scenes.summary:
The partial sums bounce between 1 and 0 forever in this scene. So this series has no sum.

Add one term and the total flips from 1 to 0, then back to 1. It never settles on one value, so it does not converge. The famous one half is only the average of the partial sums. Having an average is not the same as having a sum.

For example, pick up one 🍬 candy and put it down, over and over without end. Holding and not holding alternate forever, so you cannot say the candy is simply there.

scenes.title: Dirichlet's Test
scenes.summary:
A wobbling series gets tamed by a sinking weight in this scene. Two ingredients meet and produce convergence.

The partial sums of the sine terms wobble around but stay trapped inside a fixed fence. Multiply them by weights that sink to 0. The wobble gets pressed flatter and flatter until the series converges. The test's exact conditions are in the formulas below.

For example, a ⚽ ball bounces around inside a fence and never escapes. Push it more and more gently, and its wandering dies down until it settles.

scenes.title: Abel's Test
scenes.summary:
A convergent series stays convergent when multiplied by a monotone weight here. This test is the companion of Dirichlet's test.

The weight sequence only needs to move in one direction and stay bounded. Unlike in Dirichlet's test, it does not have to tend to 0. The secret is rewriting the product sum using partial sums and weight differences. The weight's small steps then pile up under control.

For example, a 🏪 shop nudges its prices in one direction only, a little each day. If the running total of items sold has already settled, the running revenue settles along with it.

scenes.title: Double Series and Fubini
scenes.summary:
Numbers on a grid get summed by rows first, then by columns, in this scene. With absolute convergence, the two answers agree.

Add along the rows or down the columns: the result is one and the same. The order cannot change it because the absolute values sum to a finite total. With only conditional convergence, swapping the order changes the answer itself. The headline value is the second formula below.

For example, stack 📦 boxes in a grid and count the items inside each box. Count row by row or column by column — the total count comes out identical.

scenes.title: Power Series and Radius of Convergence
scenes.summary:
Where does a power series converge, and where does it fall apart?

Inside the radius lies a safe zone. There the series converges even with absolute values. Outside, the terms themselves fail to shrink to zero. Points on the boundary each have their own fate.

For example, think of Wi-Fi in a 🏠 house. It works well inside and drops as you walk away. Right at the door it may or may not connect, so you check case by case.

scenes.title: Hadamard Gap Theorem
scenes.summary:
What happens at the boundary when a series has growing gaps?

Exponents doubling like 1, 2, 4, 8 leave bigger and bigger holes. The holes block continuation to every point of the circle. This happens even though the series converges nicely inside. The gap-free comparison series stays calm.

For example, imagine a 🪜 staircase whose steps spread by 1, 2, 4, 8. The first steps are easy. Soon one step is too far, and the wall's end is out of reach.

scenes.title: Abel's Theorem
scenes.summary:
Does the sum of a series match the limit of its power series at 1?

If the series converges, the power series heads to the same value as x nears 1, as in the formula below. Even the divergent Grandi series points to one half in this limit. But that value is an Abel sum, a separate convention, not the sum.

For example, imagine a 🧑 friend shouting 1 and 0 in turns. If each shout is a bit quieter than the last, the running average settles near one half.

scenes.title: Tauber's Theorem
scenes.summary:
If an Abel sum exists, must the ordinary sum exist too?

Only under an extra condition. The terms must shrink faster than one over n. Grandi's series breaks it, since its terms never shrink. When the condition holds, the Abel-sum curve reaches the ordinary sum.

For example, think of walking to the door of a 🏠 house. Your steps must keep shrinking to stop right at the door. Steps that never shrink just carry you past it, back and forth.

scenes.title: Two Roads to e
scenes.summary:
Two roads lead to e — which one gets there faster?

The compound-growth road creeps forward step by step. The factorial series has terms that shrink almost instantly. A handful of terms already pins down many digits.

For example, think of 💰 money in a 🐷 piggy bank earning interest on its interest. More rounds push it toward e, but the series arrives far sooner.

scenes.title: ζ(4) and Even Powers
scenes.summary:
What do the reciprocals of fourth powers add up to?

The partial sums hug the answer after only a few terms. Fourth powers shrink the tail to almost nothing. At every even power, the closed answer is a power of pi times a fraction.

For example, picture stacking 🍰 cake slices that shrink fast. Each slice is soon tiny, so a few slices fix the total height.

scenes.title: Rearranging Changes the Sum
scenes.summary:
What happens to the sum when we reorder a conditionally convergent series?

Positive terms and negative terms both pile up without end. So choosing which side to draw from first pushes the sum around. Nothing like this happens when the absolute series converges.

For example, think of putting 💰 coins into a 🐷 piggy bank and taking them out. If both piles of coins are endless, the order alone changes the balance.

scenes.title: Absolute Convergence
scenes.summary:
If the absolute-value series converges, must the original follow?

A finite absolute total settles everything. The signed partial sums wobble inside it and land on one point. In reverse, alternating signs can rescue a series whose absolute total diverges.

For example, picture a 🧑 person stepping forward, then a little back. If all the step lengths add to a finite total, the walker ends up standing somewhere definite.

scenes.title: Riemann's Rearrangement Theorem
scenes.summary:
Can rearranging alone manufacture any sum we want?

The greedy rule is simple. Below the target, take a positive term; above it, take a negative one. The terms shrink, so each overshoot shrinks too. That is why any real target can be hit exactly.

For example, think of steering a 🚗 car. Turn more when short of the spot, back when past it. Small corrections land you exactly where you aim.

scenes.title: The Cauchy Product
scenes.summary:
How do the terms pair up when two series are multiplied?

Each product term gathers pairs along a diagonal of the lattice, as in the formula below. If one side converges absolutely, the product lands on the product of the sums. If both converge only conditionally, the diagonal sums can collapse.

For example, picture 📦 boxes in a grid, picked up one diagonal at a time. If the boxes shrink fast enough, the basket's total settles down.

scenes.title: The Weierstrass M-Test
scenes.summary:
One test that settles uniform convergence of a series of functions all at once.

The key is a cap that dominates each term at every point. If the caps themselves sum finitely, the tail shrinks across the whole interval together. So the error band tightens everywhere at once.

For example, think of 📦 box lids covering every item. If the lid sizes add up finitely, nothing can poke out anywhere.

scenes.title: Dini's Theorem
scenes.summary:
When does pointwise convergence of a monotone family upgrade to uniform?

On a closed interval, it does. Monotonicity means no function falls behind once it catches up. The waiting times at all points tie into one finite bound. So the whole family closes in together.

For example, think of climbing a 🪜 staircase. If nobody steps back, reaching the last step means the whole group has arrived.

scenes.title: The Ringing That Never Dies
scenes.summary:
Round sine waves are layered to build a sharp square wave.

More terms press the flat parts onto the wave. But the ringing beside each jump does not shrink. No number of terms removes that bump.

For example, zoom into a 🏢 building in a 📷 photo. Smaller pixels sharpen the shape. Yet the jagged marks along the edges stay to the end.

scenes.title: Riemann–Lebesgue Lemma
scenes.summary:
What happens to Fourier coefficients as oscillation speeds up?

A rapidly wiggling wave averages away the function's bumps. Within one wavelength the function looks nearly constant. So as the frequency grows, every coefficient dies to zero.

For example, shake a 🧵 string very fast. The wiggle blurs into a faint band, the ups and downs cancelling to leave only the middle.

scenes.title: Fejér's Theorem
scenes.summary:
What happens when the ringing Fourier partial sums are averaged?

Averaging the partial sums cancels their bumps against each other. The averaging kernel is positive and piled sharply at the center. So the averages settle onto the function across the whole interval at once.

For example, overlay several shaky 📷 photos. Each photo's wobble cancels in the stack, and the picture turns clear.

scenes.title: Parseval's Identity
scenes.summary:
Is a function's energy captured exactly on the coefficient side?

The function's total square equals the coefficients' total square, as in the formula below. Adding modes pushes the captured share of energy toward all of it. Nothing is lost and nothing is invented.

For example, count the 💰 coins in a 🐷 piggy bank by denomination and add them up. Changing how you count never changes the total.

scenes.title: The Gibbs Phenomenon
scenes.summary:
Why does the bump beside a jump refuse to die?

Zooming into the bump collapses every case onto one curve. Its first peak is fixed near 1.179. More terms narrow the bump but never lower it.

For example, zoom into the corner of a 📷 photo. The jagged part gets narrower as you zoom, but how far it sticks out stays the same.

scenes.title: Function Spaces: Cc, C0, Cb
scenes.summary:
This scene is about function spaces. See how the three families of continuous functions C_c, C_0, and C_b nest and split.

C_b is all bounded continuous functions. C_0 holds the ones that fade to 0 far away, and C_c the ones that are exactly 0 outside a finite interval. Both inclusions C_c \subset C_0 \subset C_b are strict.

For example, a ⛺ tent stands on a finite patch of ground. Fog thins out with distance but lies everywhere. An endless plain never fades away at all.

scenes.title: Differentiable Implies Continuous
scenes.summary:
Differentiable implies continuous, but not the other way around. This scene zooms into the corner that shows why.

Continuous only means the graph has no breaks. Differentiable asks for more. The tangent slope must settle to a single value. At a sharp corner the slope splits into two.

For example, a 🚗 car climbing a smooth hill has a speed at every moment. But on a path with a sharp zigzag corner, the speed at the corner is not one single value.

scenes.title: A Discontinuous Derivative
scenes.summary:
A function differentiable everywhere whose derivative alone is discontinuous. Zoom near the origin to watch the derivative oscillate.

The function itself settles smoothly at the origin. Its slope, though, never stops oscillating. Differentiable does not force the derivative to be continuous. Still, the derivative never skips an intermediate value.

For example, picture a ⚽ ball bouncing lower and faster each time it hits the floor. Its height calmly sinks to zero. Its bounce speed, though, keeps flickering to the very end.

scenes.title: The Secant Meets Its Parallel Tangent
scenes.summary:
Somewhere on the curve sits a tangent parallel to the secant. This scene lets you hunt for that point.

The secant's slope is the average rate of change. At some interior point the instantaneous slope matches it exactly. That is what the mean value theorem guarantees.

For example, a 🚗 car covering 100 km in one hour averages 100 km/h. At some moment in that hour, the speedometer read exactly 100.

scenes.title: Derivative Sign and Monotonicity
scenes.summary:
The sign of the derivative decides where the curve rises and falls. Drag the point and watch the tangent's color track the sign.

Where the slope is positive, the curve climbs. Where it is negative, the curve drops. Reading the sign alone reveals the monotone stretches. The mean value theorem proves this link.

For example, while you climb a 🪜 staircase your height keeps growing. While you go down, it keeps shrinking. The tilt alone tells you whether you rise or fall.

scenes.title: The Inverse Function Theorem
scenes.summary:
Near a point with nonzero slope, a function can be flipped. The flipped function's slope is the reciprocal of the original.

Flipping swaps horizontal and vertical. So the ratio of rise to run turns upside down. Multiply the two tangent slopes and you get exactly 1.

For example, imagine 💰 money and 🍬 candies traded at a 🏪 shop: 4 money for 1 candy. Traded back, 1 money buys a quarter of a candy — the rate flips into its reciprocal.

scenes.title: Cauchy's Mean Value Theorem
scenes.summary:
The mean value theorem survives on parametric curves, where two functions move together. A tangent parallel to the chord always exists.

Track the change of one quantity against another. Somewhere, the instantaneous ratio equals the whole interval's ratio. This is the bridge that proves l'Hôpital's rule.

For example, a 🚗 car climbing a mountain road gains distance and height together. At some moment it climbs at exactly the trip's overall height-to-distance ratio.

scenes.title: L'Hôpital's Rule
scenes.summary:
This scene tackles limits that look like 0 divided by 0. Differentiate top and bottom separately and the limit appears.

When both sides shrink to zero, amounts stop deciding the ratio. What matters is which one shrinks faster. Comparing the two speeds gives the answer.

For example, when two puddles of 💧 water both dry up, their remaining ratio is not set by the starting amounts. It is set by the ratio of their drying speeds.

scenes.title: Darboux's Theorem
scenes.summary:
A derivative keeps the intermediate value property even when discontinuous. Watch a wildly oscillating derivative step on every level.

A derivative cannot jump across values. To get from one value to another it must pass through everything between. Even a discontinuous derivative obeys this rule.

For example, a 🌡️ thermometer sliding from −1° to 1° passes through every temperature between. A derivative likewise never jumps over an intermediate value.

scenes.title: The Weierstrass Function
scenes.summary:
A function continuous everywhere yet differentiable nowhere. Add partial sums and the graph grows thornier.

Ordinary curves flatten when you zoom in. This one grows fresh teeth at every magnification. So no point ever earns a tangent line. Uniform convergence powers the continuity half.

For example, zoom into a 🌳 tree branch and smaller twigs appear, then smaller still, forever. At no magnification does the jaggedness smooth away.

scenes.title: Polynomials Hugging the Curve
scenes.summary:
This scene lays a polynomial over a curve. Raise the degree and it hugs the curve.

Match the value, the slope, and the bending at one point. The more you match, the better the imitation nearby. Far away, the imitation eventually breaks.

For example, knowing where a 🚗 car is, how fast it goes, and how it accelerates lets you predict its position a little later. More information predicts farther ahead.

scenes.title: Taylor's Theorem: The Remainder Envelope
scenes.summary:
This scene shows the band that traps the Taylor error. Raise the degree and the band shrinks to zero.

The remainder has a ceiling. So you can promise in advance how large the error can get. The true curve always stays inside the band.

For example, measuring with a 📏 ruler promises an error of at most a millimeter. The Taylor remainder makes the same kind of promise. Higher degree narrows the promised range.

scenes.title: Convex Functions
scenes.summary:
This scene studies functions whose chords float above the graph. Convexity turns out to be the derivative increasing.

Picture a bowl shape opening upward. A curve whose slope keeps growing is convex. The middle height never exceeds the average of the end heights.

For example, stretch a 🧵 string taut between two points on a bowl-shaped curve and it always floats above the curve. The string's middle sits higher than the curve's middle.

scenes.title: Riding Tangents to the Root
scenes.summary:
Ride tangent lines down to a root. Each iteration doubles the number of correct digits.

Draw the tangent and take its root as the next guess. A straight line stands in for the curve. From a good start, the guesses converge astonishingly fast.

For example, guessing a number a 🧑 friend hid, each hint doubles the correct digits of your next guess. A wild first guess turns exact within a few rounds.

scenes.title: The Contraction Cobweb
scenes.summary:
A cobweb spirals into a single point. That point is the fixed point.

Repeatedly apply a map that shrinks distances by a fixed ratio. The points crowd closer and closer together. In the end only one point can remain.

For example, nest a smaller 📦 box inside a box, then a smaller one inside that, and the boxes close in on a single point. Each step leaves less room than the last.

scenes.title: The Gamma Function
scenes.summary:
The factorial stretched to real arguments. Values that jumped like stairs become one smooth curve.

The key rule: shifting by one multiplies by the shift amount. That rule fills in the values between integers. An integral, an area, draws the whole curve.

For example, picture a 🪜 staircase jumping 1, 2, 6, 24, with a smooth slide fitted between its steps. Now the heights between steps can be measured too.

scenes.title: The Beta Function
scenes.summary:
The area under a curve shaped by two exponents, p and q, is the beta function. Sliders morph the curve's shape.

The two ends of the curve are pulled with different strengths. So the hump shifts and changes height. This area equals an exact ratio of gamma functions.

For example, pull the two ends of a 🧵 string with different strengths and the bulge in the middle changes shape. Adjusting the end pulls is what p and q do.

scenes.title: Bohr–Mollerup Theorem
scenes.summary:
Two rules alone do not pin down the factorial's extension. An impostor matching the gamma function at every integer survives.

One extra condition filters the impostor out: log-convexity. The graph of the logarithm must be convex. The secant test exposes this fingerprint.

For example, height and weight alone cannot confirm a 🧑 friend's identity. A matching fingerprint settles it. Log-convexity is the gamma function's fingerprint.

scenes.title: Improper Integrals
scenes.summary:
Integrals over intervals that run forever or blow up. The exponent p decides convergence against divergence.

An endless region can still have finite area. Its tail just has to thin out fast enough. Too thick a tail piles area up forever.

For example, a 💧 water leak that slows down quickly spills only one bucketful, even leaking forever. A leak that slows too little overflows the bucket in the end.

scenes.title: Gabriel's Horn
scenes.summary:
Spin a curve into a horn and meet a paradox. The volume is finite but the surface area is infinite.

Filling the inside and painting the outside behave differently. The thinning rate splits the two computations. One total stops growing while the other never does.

For example, a coiled 🧵 string fits inside a small 📦 box. Spread that same string flat across the floor and it would need an endless room.

scenes.title: Upper and Lower Sums Close In
scenes.summary:
Rectangles pack the region under a curve to measure its area. Lower and upper sums squeeze the true area from both sides.

The answer sits between the underfilled and overfilled totals. Finer partitions narrow the gap between them. When the gap vanishes, that value is the integral.

For example, fit square pieces into the curved shape of a 🍰 cake. The smaller you cut the pieces, the fewer gaps remain and the better they match.

scenes.title: The Dirichlet Function
scenes.summary:
A function that is 1 on the rationals and 0 on the irrationals. It is the canonical failure of the Riemann integral.

Every tiny interval holds rationals and irrationals together. So the upper sum stays pinned at 1. The lower sum stays at 0 and the gap never closes.

For example, mix black and white ⚽ balls as finely as you like, and every scoop still holds both colors. No single height can be assigned.

scenes.title: Volterra's Function
scenes.summary:
Differentiable everywhere with a bounded derivative, yet that derivative is not Riemann integrable. Bumps rise over a fat Cantor set.

The function itself joins up smoothly. The trouble is its derivative, oscillating hard on a thick set. Riemann sums cannot capture that oscillation.

For example, measure the slope of a smooth road with a 📏 ruler, but the reading jumps wherever the ruler touches. The road is fine; the measurement fails.

scenes.title: The Area Function's Derivative Is the Function
scenes.summary:
Measure the slope of the accumulated-area function. It matches the original function exactly.

Area grows at a rate equal to the height at that point. Nudge the right edge and a thin strip attaches. The strip's area is height times the nudge.

For example, filling a tank with 💧 water, the level rises at the rate the water pours in. Differentiate what has accumulated and you recover what is pouring.

scenes.title: Integration by Parts
scenes.summary:
Run the product rule backwards to trade one integral for another. The area splits into two pieces, each computed separately.

A hard integral becomes a boundary term plus an easier integral. In the area picture, one big rectangle splits into two pieces. Both computations agree to the last decimal.

For example, measuring a 🍰 cake's area gets easier when you swap to a full rectangle minus one piece. Split the measuring and even awkward shapes become manageable.

scenes.title: Change of Variables
scenes.summary:
Stretch and squeeze the axis to rewrite an integral. Two different substitutions land on the same value.

Change the scale and the endpoints move along. Areas need correcting by the stretch factor. After the correction, a hard integral turns easy.

For example, measure with a 📏 ruler whose marks are stretched twofold and every reading doubles. Halving the reading corrects it back to the true length.

scenes.title: Functions of Bounded Variation
scenes.summary:
This scene measures the total distance a function wiggles. If that sum stays under a finite ceiling, the function has bounded variation.

Start and finish alone are not enough. Every up and down in between must be added. Monotone functions pass since they wiggle one way only. Endless trembling makes the sum explode.

For example, a 🚗 car driving up and down has bounded variation while its total mileage stays definite. Trembling in place forever would pile the distance up without end.

scenes.title: Arc Length
scenes.summary:
This scene measures a curve by cutting it into straight pieces. The sum of the piece lengths is the polygonal length.

Finer partitions only make that sum grow, approaching the true length from below. The supremum over all partitions is the length of the curve. If that supremum is infinite, the curve cannot be measured.

For example, lay a 🧵 string along a winding path and measure it piece by piece, straightening each bit. The finer the pieces, the closer you get to the string's true length.

scenes.title: The Riemann–Stieltjes Integral
scenes.summary:
An integral that weighs intervals by the integrator's growth, not their length. Change the integrator and the same intervals count differently.

Each interval can carry a different weight. A step integrator dumps all its weight on one point. Then the integral is decided by that point alone.

For example, total cargo by weight, not by count, when each 📦 box weighs differently. If one box holds all the weight, it alone decides the total.

scenes.title: Jordan Decomposition
scenes.summary:
Every bounded-variation function splits into a difference of two increasing functions. Drag the probe and watch the identity hold pointwise.

Record the total rise and the total fall separately. Subtract falls from rises to get the current height. The variation function is the running record of rises.

For example, money now in a 🐷 piggy bank is the total 💰 money put in minus the total taken out. Rises and falls are counted on separate tallies.

scenes.title: Lebesgue Measure
scenes.summary:
The cheapest interval cover prices a set's size. A single point, and even all the rationals, cost nothing.

Length measurement extends to sets like points and rationals. Among all covers, take the smallest total length. That smallest total is the set's size.

For example, cover a set with pieces of 🧵 string; the shortest total string length is the set's size. A single point needs almost no string, so its size is zero.

scenes.title: The Vitali Set
scenes.summary:
Pick one representative from each equivalence class using the axiom of choice. The result is a set whose size cannot be measured.

Shifted copies of this set cover a whole interval. If its size were zero, the copies would total zero. If positive, the copies would total infinity. Both contradict, so no size exists.

For example, copies of one 📦 box can fill a room, yet if the box's size were zero the total should be zero, and if it were anything more the total would explode. So the size cannot be assigned.

scenes.title: Borel–Cantelli Lemmas
scenes.summary:
If total length is finite, points hit infinitely often form a null set. This scene checks that boundary numerically.

Collect the points where the events keep overlapping. Finite total length makes the overlaps rarer and rarer. With independence, the converse also holds.

For example, in rain whose 💧 water drops keep shrinking, a finite total volume means one spot is almost never hit endlessly.

scenes.title: Covering the Rationals with Nothing
scenes.summary:
Cover the rationals one by one and the total length drops below any bound. The Riemann integral cannot move here.

The rationals are countably many. So they can be numbered and given shrinking covers. The covers' total can be made as small as you wish.

For example, cover 🍬 candies scattered on the floor, one by one, with smaller and smaller cups, and the cups' total size shrinks as low as you like.

scenes.title: Lebesgue Convergence Theorems
scenes.summary:
Three theorems license swapping limits and integrals. Examples with escaping mass show why each hypothesis is needed.

Swapping the order requires that no mass leaks away. A dominating function overhead keeps things safe. Without conditions, area can vanish in the limit.

For example, pour 💧 water from cup to cup with no spill and the total stays the same. One drop escaping sideways shrinks the total that arrives.

scenes.title: Fubini–Tonelli Theorem
scenes.summary:
Iterated integrals agree in either order. Sum the rows first or the columns first, the total is the same.

For nonnegative functions this is always safe. For integrable functions it is safe too. Without integrability, the two orders can split apart.

For example, count 🍎 apples packed in a grid inside a 📦 box: counting by rows or by columns gives the same total.

scenes.title: Convolution
scenes.summary:
Flip one function, slide it, and measure how it overlaps the other. Overlapping two indicator blocks gives an overlap length that traces a tent curve.

Convolving with a smooth kernel softens even a sharp step function. The narrower the kernel, the closer the softened function sits to the original.

For example, it is the blur effect in a 📷 photo, replacing each pixel by a weighted average of its neighbors. The center pixel gets the largest weight.

scenes.title: Egorov's Theorem
scenes.summary:
On a finite-measure set, pointwise convergence is almost uniform. Squeeze the bad set small and the rest converges uniformly.

The slow points hide inside one small set. Remove that set and the rest converges at one pace. The whole space must have finite measure.

For example, of 30 🧑 friends racing to a finish line, one or two may lag; set them aside and the rest arrive at nearly the same pace.

scenes.title: Absolute Continuity
scenes.summary:
Shrink the total length of intervals to zero and the total change shrinks too. The Cantor function is a continuous function failing this.

Tiny input changes must not create large outputs. Such functions are exactly the ones built as integrals. The Cantor function stays flat yet climbs from 0 to 1, breaking the rule.

For example, open a tap a little and only a little 💧 water comes out. The Cantor function is a strange tap that pours a bucketful while barely opened.

scenes.title: Differentiation Under the Integral Sign
scenes.summary:
Numerics confirm that differentiating inside the integral matches the tangent slope. Drag the point and its tangent along the curve.

Differentiating the whole or the inside gives the same answer. Each point's change accumulates into the total change. A domination condition makes the swap safe.

For example, measure how fast a room's average 🌡️ thermometer reading rises: averaging how fast each spot warms up gives the same answer.

scenes.title: Minkowski's Inequality
scenes.summary:
The size of a sum of two functions never exceeds the sum of their sizes. Slide the exponent p and the gap between the bars opens and closes.

This is the triangle inequality moved to functions. A straight route is never longer than two joined legs. At exponent 1 the gap closes completely.

For example, a 🚗 car that drives two legs in an L shape travels at least the straight-line distance, never more than the two legs added together.

terms.definition: A statement that is either true or false — proof is the art of combining propositions with connectives and tracking how the truth values are forced.
A proof that takes the hypothesis as given and reaches the conclusion by a straight chain of justified steps — no detours.
Splitting the domain into cases that cover everything, and proving the claim in each case — together the cases cover the whole proof.
terms.sceneTitle: Proof by Cases and Existence Proofs

terms.definition: g \circ f — apply f first, then g to the result. Injectivity and surjectivity propagate through composition in provable ways.
\forall (for all) and \exists (there exists) — the symbols that pin down precisely how a statement ranges over its domain. Negation swaps the two.
The contrapositive of P \Rightarrow Q is \lnot Q \Rightarrow \lnot P — always equivalent to the original, so it can be proved in its place when the direct route stalls.
The method that assumes the negation of the conclusion and derives a contradiction — if assuming \lnot P yields a contradiction (\bot), then P holds.
P \iff Q — an "if and only if" claim that is completed only by proving the two directions P \Rightarrow Q and Q \Rightarrow P separately.
terms.sceneTitle: Counterexamples and If and Only If

terms.definition: Induction that assumes all of P(2), \dots, P(n-1) when proving P(n) — used when the step needs much smaller values, like the factors of n.
A relation that is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive — its equivalence classes partition the whole set without overlap.
1, 2, 3, \dots — the basic unit of counting, axiomatized by Peano.
The proof principle getting P(n) for every natural n from P(1) and P(k) \Rightarrow P(k+1) — like dominoes falling in turn.
The five axioms defining the naturals — existence of 1, the successor function, the induction axiom, and more. Addition and multiplication are defined recursively from them.
\binom{n}{k} = \frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!} — the number of ways to choose k from n. Satisfies Pascal's identity \binom{n}{k}+\binom{n}{k-1}=\binom{n+1}{k}.
(x+y)^n = \sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k}x^{n-k}y^k — proved by induction, with Pascal's identity as the inductive step.
\dots, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, \dots — built as equivalence classes of natural pairs with (a,b)\sim(c,d)\iff a+d=b+c (the number "a-b").
\frac{a}{b} (b \ne 0) — built as equivalence classes of integer pairs with (a,b)\sim(c,d)\iff ad=bc; they form a field.
The set of elements equivalent under an equivalence relation — the key technique for "building" the integers, rationals, and reals.
A collection of distinct objects. Every discussion in analysis begins with a set.
A rule assigning to each element of a domain exactly one element of a codomain.
The least of the upper bounds of a set, written \sup A.
The greatest of the lower bounds of a set, written \inf A.
The x \ge 0 with x^n = a; its existence is guaranteed by \sup\{x \ge 0 : x^n < a\}.
The axiom that a choice function exists for any collection of nonempty sets.
If every chain has an upper bound, a maximal element exists. Equivalent to the axiom of choice.
